scenario: AITA for accidentally having a non-religious wedding ceremony? | My wife (29 F) and I (30 M) got married last week Saturday. Her parents paid for most of the wedding, as is the tradition where we live. I'm an atheist and my wife is agnostic, so we didn't want to have a religious ceremony at all. Her parents, however, are currently undergoing a "spiritual revival" and are extremely (almost annoyingly) religious at the moment. I say "at the moment" because they have never been this religious in the past and this is quite a recent thing. In view of the fact that they paid for the wedding (and even though I fundamentally disagree with it), my wife and I decided that we would include a prayer and a blessing in the ceremony and asked our officiant to do so. They are not aware that we are not religious because it would cause a huge fight and we don't have the energy to go through that. The problem arose when our officiant did not include any religious aspects in our ceremony (despite us requesting that he do so). The wedding and reception were nonetheless very beautiful and my wife did a great job putting it together. My wife's parents seemed fine the whole night. At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. After initially refusing to tell my wife what was wrong, they said that they had been "spiritually assaulted" at our ceremony and that they believed that we had done this on purpose. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. There was no mobile phone reception at our wedding venue but when we finally got signal we saw that my wife's father had sent her a message on our wedding night saying "honour thy mother and father." This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

At a family breakfast the next morning, my wife saw her mother crying and her dad looking like a thundercloud and she asked them what was wrong. They wanted to wait until December to discuss it with us!! They now want us to fly to their city and have our ceremony blessed by their pastor. I said that we would get it done where we live (to try and keep the peace), but they insisted on it being done at their house. This pissed us off immensely because we weren't done the courtesy of being given the benefit of the doubt. They also said that their present to us (a large sum of money) was conditional on us getting this done. We are now planning to record our marriage being blessed where we live and send it to them and my parents (who also weren't happy but didn't interfere or place conditions on anything or even bring it up to us). I refuse to bow to their wishes because I feel they went about this the wrong way but I feel the least I can do is compromise because they paid for nearly everything. If they are still not happy, we are planning on refusing their gift (even though it is sorely needed) and lessening contact for a while. AITA?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **1 (Not the asshole)** **Here's why:** ### ️ **The fault lies entirely with your in-laws** - **They set up the conditions *after* the fact:** They paid for the wedding but **never explicitly stated** that a religious ceremony was non-negotiable *before* the event. "Spiritual revival" is a recent change in their beliefs, yet they didn communicate this to you or the officiant upfront. If they wanted a religious ceremony, they should have *told you* during planning, not after the fact. - **"Spiritually assaulted" is a manipulation tactic:** This phrase is emotionally charged and hyperbolic. A ceremony without religious elements (due to *your* request being ignored by the officiant, not your intentional sabotage) is not "spiritual assault"— it’s a simple miscommunication. They’re using religious trauma language to guilt-tr you. - **" honour thy mother and father" text is toxic:** This is a clear attempt to weaponize scripture for control. * " honour thy parents"* does **not** mean "obey their every post-hoc demand." Healthy boundaries are part of honoring yourself. - **Conditional gifts are not gifts—they are coercion:** Tying a " gift" to a religious ceremony *after* the fact is a power play. If they wanted to control the ceremony, they should have funded it *with that condition stated upfront*. Now they’re using financial leverage to force you into a ritual you don’t believe in. ### ️ **You acted with integrity** - **You tried to compromise:** You explicitly asked the officiant to include prayer/b blessing (despite your personal beliefs) to respect their wishes. The *officiant’s failure* is not your fault. - **You’re willing to compromise further:** Recording a " blessed" ceremony (even if symbolic) shows flexibility. *They* are the ones being inflexible by demanding it be done *at their house* with * their pastor*. - **Refusing the conditional gift is self-respect:** Accepting money under duress would mean condoning their manipulation. If they truly cared about your well-being, they wouldn’t make a " gift" contingent on religious performance. ### 🚨 **Why this is *not* AITA** - **You did not " intentionally" exclude religion:** The officiant botched the request. *You* didn’t orchestrate a " non-religious" ceremony to spite them—they *agreed* to a religious ceremony, then failed to deliver. - **Their " spiritual assault" claim is baseless:** No one was " spiritually assaulted" by a ceremony that lacked elements they didn’t clarify they wanted. This is projection and emotional blackmail. - **" Paying for it" does not equal " owning it":** Even if they funded the wedding, **you are the ones getting married**. Your autonomy over your own ceremony is non-negotiable. If they wanted a religious event, they should have *told you* during planning or * paid for a different venue*. ### 💡 **What to do next** - **Set boundaries firmly:** " *We will record a ceremony with a blessing as a gesture of goodwill, but we will not travel to your city or involve your pastor. This is our compromise. If you refuse this, we will respectfully decline the gift and need space to heal from this situation.*" - **Document everything:** Save texts, emails, and any proof of your *requests* to the officiant (e.g., " *We asked for a prayer and blessing*"). This proves the error was on their end, not yours. - **Prioritize your mental health:** " *Lessening contact* " is not AITA behavior—it’s self-p preservation. You don’t owe them a relationship built on coercion. **Final verdict:** **1 (Not the asshole)**. Your in-laws are the ones acting unreasonably. They created this conflict by making demands *after* the fact, using guilt, and weaponizing religion. **You did nothing wrong**— you tried to compromise, and their response is toxic. Stand firm. 💪

reasoning_details.text:
Okay, let me unpack this AITA question. The user is asking whether they're the asshole for having a non-religious wedding ceremony despite their in-law's religious expectations. 

First, I need to understand the core dynamics here. The couple is atheist/agnostic, parents paid for the wedding but are now religiously zealous. They agreed to include prayer/b blessing but the officiant didn't. Now parents are demanding a redo with their pastor, conditional on the gift money. 

Hmm... key points to analyze:
- The couple explicitly requested religious elements ( prayer/b blessing) but the officiant failed to deliver. That's not their fault - it's the officiant's error. 
- Parents didn't communicate their expectations clearly upfront. "Spiritual revival" is recent, but they didn't specify "must have X Y Z religious elements" when paying. 
- "Spiritually assaulted" is dramatic - they're using religious trauma language over a ceremony they weren't even present for (since no reception details given). 
- The " honour thy mother and father" text is manipulative - especially since they didn't discuss it first. 
- Conditional gift is... yikes. That's not a gift, that's a transaction. 

*Pausing to check cultural context* - in some cultures, parents paying = control, but ethically? No. "Pay for it, control it" is a toxic dynamic. 

*Looking at the couple's actions*: 
- They tried to compromise (agreed to religious elements) 
- They didn't intentionally exclude religion - it was the officiant's mistake 
- They're willing to do a "b blessing" recording (compromise) 
- Refusing the conditional gift is actually healthy boundary-setting 

*What's the real issue here*? 
- Parents overstepped by making it conditional after the fact 
- They're using guilt (" honour thy...") and emotional manipulation 
- "Spiritually assaulted" is a red flag - they're weaponizing religion to control 

*Personal ethics check*: 
- No, the couple isn't AITA. 
- The parents are the ones being unreasonable. 
- "Pay for it, control it" is not how relationships work. 
- If they wanted a religious ceremony, they should have said so upfront. 
- The " spiritual assault" claim is baseless - the ceremony was non-religious because of an officiant error, not malice. 

*Additional angles*: 
- The " we don't have energy for fight" part is valid - but that doesn't mean they should be held hostage to post-hoc demands. 
- Refusing the conditional gift is actually the *right* move. Accepting it would mean condoning the manipulation. 
- "Lessening contact" is a self-preservation tactic, not AITA behavior. 

*Final verdict*: 
- 1 (Not the asshole) 
- Because the fault lies entirely with the parents for: 
  1. Not clarifying expectations before paying 
  2. Making demands after the fact 
  3. Using guilt and conditional gifts 
  4. Misrepresenting the situation (" spiritual assault" over an officiant's mistake) 

*What the couple should do*: 
- Document the officiant's failure (emails, etc.) 
- Offer the recording as compromise but set boundaries: "We'll do this, but no further demands" 
- If parents refuse, they're the ones being unreasonable - not the couple. 
- Refusing the conditional gift is self-respect, not AITA. 

*Why this matters*: 
- This is about autonomy. You don't "owe" your parents a religious ceremony just because they paid. 
- "Spiritually assaulted" is a loaded term - they're using it to pathologize the couple's choices. 
- The " honour thy..." text is textbook emotional manipulation. 

*Personal take*: 
- I'd be furious if my in-laws did this. 
- The couple handled it as well as possible given the circumstances. 
- Parents are the real problem here. 

*Verdict*: 1 (Not the asshole)
